answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer:
No, skip the 16-miler. Six days before the race it would add fatigue and very little fitness, so you would start on tired legs. Your fitness is already built: your easy pace has held near 9:52/mi at 139 bpm for four weeks, and your 20-mile run on Sun Oct 4 was the last big test.

Flat legs and worry about losing fitness are common once the volume drops in a taper. They usually ease in the last few days, and the short marathon-pace session on Wed Oct 14 keeps the rhythm without adding load.

new.analysis:
## What the week showed
Every planned day was run, with no skipped sessions and no extra runs. The week of Oct 5 – 11 came to 34 miles, down from 46, and the long run fell from 20 miles to 12. That step down is the taper working as intended.

Easy running stayed steady. Easy pace held near 9:52/mi and average heart rate at 139 bpm, the same as four weeks ago. Your aerobic base is intact, even though the legs feel heavy.

Time in easy zones was 67.5 percent, below the 80 percent target. That came mostly from the Wednesday session and the time in zone 3 on the 12-mile long run, which is reasonable for a week with one hard session and a long run. The long run itself was steady, with heart rate rising only 7 bpm.

## The overrun
The Wednesday session was meant to hold four marathon-pace reps, and seven were run. Pace stayed on target near 8:36/mi, so the extra work was more hard running rather than faster running. That extra load is a likely reason the legs feel heavy now, and the fix is to keep this week easy.

## Why this plan
This week carries 20 miles of training before the race, about 40 percent of your peak week. That is enough to keep the rhythm and clear fatigue without adding load.

Quality sits on one day, Wednesday, with easy days on either side, and the two rest days stay as real rest. Short strides on Tuesday and Saturday keep leg speed sharp without adding fatigue.

## Race pace
Under 3:45 means averaging 8:35/mi or faster for 26.2 miles. Your longest runs ran near 10:00/mi, so holding goal pace over distance has not been tested yet. Starting fast costs more than starting a few seconds slow, so the first miles are where the race is won or lost.

| Miles | Pace |
| --- | --- |
| 1 – 6 | 8:40 – 8:45/mi |
| 7 – 20 | 8:30 – 8:35/mi |
| 21 – 26.2 | 8:30 – 8:35/mi, push only if the effort still feels controlled |

If it is warm on the day, let the pace slide by a few seconds per mile rather than push through it.
